en: [Book 2] [the Golden Thread]

raw: CHAPTER I. Five Years Later
en: [Chapter 1] Five Years Later

raw: Tellson’s Bank by Temple Bar was an old-fashioned place, even in the year one thousand seven hundred and eighty.
en: Tellson’s Bank near Temple Bar was an old-fashioned place, even in the year 1780.

raw: It was very small, very dark, very ugly, very incommodious.
en: It was very small, very dark, very ugly, and very uncomfortable.

raw: It was an old-fashioned place, moreover, in the moral attribute that the partners in the House were proud of its smallness, proud of its darkness, proud of its ugliness, proud of its incommodiousness.
en: Moreover, it was old-fashioned in a very particular way. The bank owners were actually proud of its smallness, its darkness, its ugliness, and its total lack of comfort.

raw: They were even boastful of its eminence in those particulars, and were fired by an express conviction that, if it were less objectionable, it would be less respectable.
en: They even bragged about how extreme these qualities were, believing that if the bank were any cleaner or more convenient, it would somehow be less respectable.

raw: This was no passive belief, but an active weapon which they flashed at more convenient places of business.
en: This was not just a quiet belief, but an active argument they used against more modern and convenient businesses.

raw: Tellson’s (they said) wanted no elbow-room, Tellson’s wanted no light, Tellson’s wanted no embellishment.
en: They would say, "Tellson's doesn’t need extra space, Tellson's doesn’t need bright light, Tellson's doesn’t need fancy decorations.

raw: Noakes and Co.’s might, or Snooks Brothers’ might; but Tellson’s, thank Heaven--!
en: Other banks might need those things, but Tellson’s, thank Heaven, does not!"

raw: Any one of these partners would have disinherited his son on the question of rebuilding Tellson’s.
en: Any of these owners would have disowned his own son over the question of rebuilding or modernizing Tellson's Bank.

raw: In this respect the House was much on a par with the Country; which did very often disinherit its sons for suggesting improvements in laws and customs that had long been highly objectionable, but were only the more respectable.
en: In this regard, the bank was very much like the country itself. England often punished its citizens for suggesting improvements to old laws and customs. Those laws had long been deeply problematic. But they were kept simply because they were old.

raw: Thus it had come to pass, that Tellson’s was the triumphant perfection of inconvenience.
en: Thus, Tellson’s had become the ultimate example of inconvenience.

raw: After bursting open a door of idiotic obstinacy with a weak rattle in its throat, you fell into Tellson’s down two steps, and came to your senses in a miserable little shop, with two little counters, where the oldest of men made your cheque shake as if the wind rustled it, while they examined the signature by the dingiest of windows, which were always under a shower-bath of mud from Fleet-street, and which were made the dingier by their own iron bars proper, and the heavy shadow of Temple Bar.
en: After pushing open a stubborn door that shook with a weak rattle, you fell down two steps into the bank. There you found yourself in a miserable little shop with two small counters. The oldest clerks working there would take your check with hands that shook so much the paper rustled like leaves, while they examined your signature by the dirtiest windows. These windows were constantly sprayed with mud from Fleet Street and made even darker by heavy iron bars and the shadow of the nearby Temple Bar gate.

raw: If your business necessitated your seeing “the House,” you were put into a species of Condemned Hold at the back, where you meditated on a misspent life, until the House came with its hands in its pockets, and you could hardly blink at it in the dismal twilight.
en: If your business required meeting with "the owners," you were escorted to a dark, prison-like room at the back. There you could meditate on your sins. You would wait there until they finally appeared ,  hands in their pockets ,  as if they had all the time in the world.

raw: Your money came out of, or went into, wormy old wooden drawers, particles of which flew up your nose and down your throat when they were opened and shut.
en: Your money came out of or went into rotting old wooden drawers, sending clouds of dust up your nose and down your throat whenever they were opened.

raw: Your bank-notes had a musty odour, as if they were fast decomposing into rags again.
en: The banknotes had a musty smell, as if they were turning back into moldy rags.

raw: Your plate was stowed away among the neighbouring cesspools, and evil communications corrupted its good polish in a day or two.
en: Silverware and valuables were stored near the sewer pipes, and the damp air quickly ruined their polish.

raw: Your deeds got into extemporised strong-rooms made of kitchens and sculleries, and fretted all the fat out of their parchments into the banking-house air.
en: Important legal documents were kept in improvised vaults made from old kitchens and pantries, absorbing the greasy air.

raw: Your lighter boxes of family papers went up-stairs into a Barmecide room, that always had a great dining-table in it and never had a dinner, and where, even in the year one thousand seven hundred and eighty, the first letters written to you by your old love, or by your little children, were but newly released from the horror of being ogled through the windows, by the heads exposed on Temple Bar with an insensate brutality and ferocity worthy of Abyssinia or Ashantee.
en: Lighter boxes of family papers went upstairs into a useless dining room that had a massive table but never served any meals. Even in 1780, the old love letters and children's notes stored there had only recently been spared a grim fate. The heads of executed criminals had long been displayed on Temple Bar just outside the windows. Their dead eyes seemed to stare right into the bank. It was a cruelty worthy of the most uncivilized lands.

raw: But indeed, at that time, putting to death was a recipe much in vogue with all trades and professions, and not least of all with Tellson’s.
en: Indeed, at that time, execution was the standard solution for almost every crime, and Tellson’s Bank fully supported it.

raw: Death is Nature’s remedy for all things, and why not Legislation’s?
en: Death was nature’s remedy for all problems, so why not the law's? Consequently, the punishments were brutal and universal.

raw: Accordingly, the forger was put to Death; the utterer of a bad note was put to Death; the unlawful opener of a letter was put to Death; the purloiner of forty shillings and sixpence was put to Death; the holder of a horse at Tellson’s door, who made off with it, was put to Death; the coiner of a bad shilling was put to Death; the sounders of three-fourths of the notes in the whole gamut of Crime, were put to Death.
en: Anyone who forged a signature was put to death. Anyone who passed a bad note was put to death. Anyone who opened a letter illegally was put to death. Anyone who stole forty shillings and sixpence was put to death. Anyone who took a horse from outside Tellson's and rode off with it was put to death.

raw: Not that it did the least good in the way of prevention--it might almost have been worth remarking that the fact was exactly the reverse--but, it cleared off (as to this world) the trouble of each particular case, and left nothing else connected with it to be looked after.
en: Anyone who made a counterfeit coin was put to death. It did not prevent crime at all, in fact, the opposite was true, but it certainly cleared the case off the books and left nothing else to worry about.

raw: Thus, Tellson’s, in its day, like greater places of business, its contemporaries, had taken so many lives, that, if the heads laid low before it had been ranged on Temple Bar instead of being privately disposed of, they would probably have excluded what little light the ground floor had, in a rather significant manner.
en: Thus, Tellson's Bank had caused so many executions that something grim could be said. If all the heads of those it had prosecuted were lined up on Temple Bar, they would have blocked what little daylight reached the ground floor. Other major businesses of the era were no different.

raw: Cramped in all kinds of dim cupboards and hutches at Tellson’s, the oldest of men carried on the business gravely.
en: Cramped in dim cupboards and tiny offices, the oldest clerks carried on the bank's business.

raw: When they took a young man into Tellson’s London house, they hid him somewhere till he was old. They kept him in a dark place, like a cheese, until he had the full Tellson flavour and blue-mould upon him.
en: When they hired a young man, they hid him away in a dark place like a cheese until he grew old and developed the full, moldy Tellson flavor.

raw: Then only was he permitted to be seen, spectacularly poring over large books, and casting his breeches and gaiters into the general weight of the establishment.
en: Only then was he allowed to be seen by customers, looking solemn as he bent over large ledger books in his old-fashioned breeches and leggings.

raw: Outside Tellson’s--never by any means in it, unless called in--was an odd-job-man, an occasional porter and messenger, who served as the live sign of the house.
en: Outside Tellson’s Bank, and never allowed inside unless specifically summoned, was an odd-job man who worked as a messenger and porter, serving as the bank's living sign.

raw: He was never absent during business hours, unless upon an errand, and then he was represented by his son: a grisly urchin of twelve, who was his express image.
en: He was always there during business hours unless he was out running an errand. When he was away, his twelve-year-old son, who looked exactly like him, took his place.

raw: People understood that Tellson’s, in a stately way, tolerated the odd-job-man.
en: The bank tolerated this messenger in a dignified way.

raw: The house had always tolerated some person in that capacity, and time and tide had drifted this person to the post.
en: The business had always had someone in that role, and time had carried this particular man to the job.

raw: His surname was Cruncher, and on the youthful occasion of his renouncing by proxy the works of darkness, in the easterly parish church of Hounsditch, he had received the added appellation of Jerry.
en: His last name was Cruncher, and when he was baptized as a child in Hounsditch, he had been given the first name Jerry.

raw: The scene was Mr.
en: The scene opens at Mr.

raw: Cruncher’s private lodging in Hanging-sword-alley, Whitefriars: the time, half-past seven of the clock on a windy March morning, Anno Domini seventeen hundred and eighty. (Mr.
en: Cruncher’s private lodging in Hanging-sword Alley, Whitefriars, at half-past seven on a windy March morning in the year 1780.

raw: Cruncher himself always spoke of the year of our Lord as Anna Dominoes: apparently under the impression that the Christian era dated from the invention of a popular game, by a lady who had bestowed her name upon it.)
en: Mr. Cruncher always referred to the year of our Lord as "Anna Dominoes," apparently believing the era was named after a popular game invented by a lady of that name.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Cruncher’s apartments were not in a savoury neighbourhood, and were but two in number, even if a closet with a single pane of glass in it might be counted as one.
en: Cruncher’s rooms were not in a pleasant neighborhood. There were only two rooms, even if you counted a tiny closet with a single pane of glass.

raw: But they were very decently kept.
en: However, they were kept very clean.

raw: Early as it was, on the windy March morning, the room in which he lay abed was already scrubbed throughout; and between the cups and saucers arranged for breakfast, and the lumbering deal table, a very clean white cloth was spread.
en: Early as it was on this windy morning, the bedroom had already been scrubbed. A clean white cloth was spread on the heavy wooden table, set with cups and saucers for breakfast.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Cruncher reposed under a patchwork counterpane, like a Harlequin at home.
en: Cruncher lay asleep under a patchwork blanket, looking like a colorful clown at rest.

raw: At first, he slept heavily, but, by degrees, began to roll and surge in bed, until he rose above the surface, with his spiky hair looking as if it must tear the sheets to ribbons.
en: At first he slept heavily, but gradually he began to roll and toss in bed until his head emerged, his spiky hair looking sharp enough to tear the sheets to pieces.

raw: At which juncture, he exclaimed, in a voice of dire exasperation:
en: At that moment, he cried out in great frustration:

raw: “Bust me, if she ain’t at it agin!”
en: "Damn me, if she isn't at it again!"

raw: A woman of orderly and industrious appearance rose from her knees in a corner, with sufficient haste and trepidation to show that she was the person referred to.
en: A neat and hardworking woman rose quickly and nervously from her knees in a corner of the room, showing she was the one he was talking to.

raw: “What!” said Mr.
en: "What!" said Mr.

raw: Cruncher, looking out of bed for a boot. “You’re at it agin, are you?”
en: Cruncher, looking out from under the covers for a boot. "You're at it again, are you?"

raw: After hailing the morn with this second salutation, he threw a boot at the woman as a third.
en: After greeting the morning with this second shout, he threw a boot at the woman as a third greeting.

raw: It was a very muddy boot, and may introduce the odd circumstance connected with Mr.
en: It was a very muddy boot. This introduces a strange detail about Mr.

raw: Cruncher’s domestic economy, that, whereas he often came home after banking hours with clean boots, he often got up next morning to find the same boots covered with clay.
en: Cruncher’s household: although he often came home after bank hours with clean boots, he frequently woke up the next morning to find them covered in clay.

raw: “What,” said Mr.
en: The boot missed.

raw: Cruncher, varying his apostrophe after missing his mark--“what are you up to, Aggerawayter?”
en: Mr. Cruncher changed his tone and said, "What, what are you up to, Aggerawayter?"

raw: “I was only saying my prayers.”
en: "I was only saying my prayers," his wife replied gently.

raw: “Saying your prayers!
en: "Saying your prayers!

raw: You’re a nice woman!
en: You're a fine woman!

raw: What do you mean by flopping yourself down and praying agin me?”
en: What do you mean by dropping to your knees and praying against me?"

raw: “I was not praying against you; I was praying for you.”
en: "I was not praying against you, Jerry. I was praying for you."

raw: “You weren’t.
en: "You weren't!

raw: And if you were, I won’t be took the liberty with.
en: And even if you were, I won't have you taking such liberties.

raw: Here! your mother’s a nice woman, young Jerry, going a praying agin your father’s prosperity.
en: Look here, young Jerry! Your mother is a fine woman, praying against your father's business success.

raw: You’ve got a dutiful mother, you have, my son.
en: You have a very dutiful mother, my son.

raw: You’ve got a religious mother, you have, my boy: going and flopping herself down, and praying that the bread-and-butter may be snatched out of the mouth of her only child.”
en: You have a very religious mother, my boy, going and dropping to her knees to pray that the bread and butter be snatched right out of her own child's mouth!"

raw: Master Cruncher (who was in his shirt) took this very ill, and, turning to his mother, strongly deprecated any praying away of his personal board.
en: Young Jerry, who was standing in his shirt, took this very seriously. Turning to his mother, he strongly protested against any prayers that might take away his food.

raw: “And what do you suppose, you conceited female,” said Mr.
en: "And what do you think, you conceited woman," Mr.

raw: Cruncher, with unconscious inconsistency, “that the worth of _your_ prayers may be?
en: Cruncher said ,  with unconscious contradiction ,  "that your prayers are actually worth?

raw: Name the price that you put _your_ prayers at!”
en: Name the price you put on your prayers!"

raw: “They only come from the heart, Jerry.
en: "They only come from the heart, Jerry.

raw: They are worth no more than that.”
en: They are worth no more than that."

raw: “Worth no more than that,” repeated Mr.
en: "Worth no more than that," Mr.

raw: Cruncher. “They ain’t worth much, then.
en: Cruncher repeated. "Then they aren't worth much.

raw: Whether or no, I won’t be prayed agin, I tell you.
en: Either way, I won't be prayed against, I tell you.

raw: I can’t afford it.
en: I can't afford it.

raw: I’m not a going to be made unlucky by _your_ sneaking.
en: I'm not going to have your sneaking prayers bring me bad luck.

raw: If you must go flopping yourself down, flop in favour of your husband and child, and not in opposition to ’em.
en: If you must drop to your knees, pray for your husband and child, not against them.

raw: If I had had any but a unnat’ral wife, and this poor boy had had any but a unnat’ral mother, I might have made some money last week instead of being counter-prayed and countermined and religiously circumwented into the worst of luck.
en: If I had a normal wife, and this poor boy had a normal mother, things would be different. I might have made some money last week. Instead, I was prayed against, undermined, and religiously tricked into the worst luck imaginable.

raw: B-u-u-ust me!” said Mr.
en: Damn me!" said Mr.

raw: Cruncher, who all this time had been putting on his clothes, “if I ain’t, what with piety and one blowed thing and another, been choused this last week into as bad luck as ever a poor devil of a honest tradesman met with!
en: Cruncher, who was putting on his clothes. "Between your piety and one cursed thing after another, I've been cheated out of my luck this week as badly as any honest tradesman ever was!

raw: Young Jerry, dress yourself, my boy, and while I clean my boots keep a eye upon your mother now and then, and if you see any signs of more flopping, give me a call.
en: Young Jerry, get dressed, my boy. While I clean my boots, keep an eye on your mother. If you see her starting to pray again, call me.

raw: For, I tell you,” here he addressed his wife once more, “I won’t be gone agin, in this manner.
en: I tell you," he said, addressing his wife again, "I won't have this.

raw: I am as rickety as a hackney-coach, I’m as sleepy as laudanum, my lines is strained to that degree that I shouldn’t know, if it wasn’t for the pain in ’em, which was me and which somebody else, yet I’m none the better for it in pocket; and it’s my suspicion that you’ve been at it from morning to night to prevent me from being the better for it in pocket, and I won’t put up with it, Aggerawayter, and what do you say now!”
en: I feel as shaky as an old carriage, as sleepy as if I'd taken opium, and my muscles are so sore that I wouldn't know who I was if it weren't for the pain. Yet I haven't made a single penny from it, and I suspect you've been praying day and night to keep me poor. I won't put up with it, Aggerawayter! What do you have to say to that?"

raw: Growling, in addition, such phrases as “Ah! yes!
en: Growling other remarks like, "Oh yes!

raw: You’re religious, too.
en: You're very religious, aren't you?

raw: You wouldn’t put yourself in opposition to the interests of your husband and child, would you?
en: You wouldn't do anything to hurt your husband and child's interests, would you?

raw: Not you!” and throwing off other sarcastic sparks from the whirling grindstone of his indignation, Mr.
en: Not you!" and muttering in his anger, Mr.

raw: Cruncher betook himself to his boot-cleaning and his general preparation for business.
en: Cruncher went to clean his boots and get ready for the day.

raw: In the meantime, his son, whose head was garnished with tenderer spikes, and whose young eyes stood close by one another, as his father’s did, kept the required watch upon his mother.
en: Meanwhile, his son, whose hair had smaller spikes and whose eyes were set close together like his father's, watched his mother as ordered.

raw: He greatly disturbed that poor woman at intervals, by darting out of his sleeping closet, where he made his toilet, with a suppressed cry of “You are going to flop, mother. --Halloa, father!” and, after raising this fictitious alarm, darting in again with an undutiful grin.
en: He repeatedly startled the poor woman by jumping out of the closet where he was getting dressed, whispering, "You're about to pray, mother! Hey, father!" before disappearing back inside with a mischievous grin.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Cruncher’s temper was not at all improved when he came to his breakfast.
en: Cruncher’s temper did not improve by breakfast time.

raw: He resented Mrs.
en: He was particularly angry when Mrs.

raw: Cruncher’s saying grace with particular animosity.
en: Cruncher tried to say grace before the meal.

raw: “Now, Aggerawayter!
en: "Now, Aggerawayter!

raw: What are you up to?
en: What are you doing?

raw: At it again?”
en: At it again?"

raw: His wife explained that she had merely “asked a blessing.”
en: His wife explained that she was only asking for a blessing on the food.

raw: “Don’t do it!” said Mr.
en: "Don't do it!" said Mr.

raw: Crunches looking about, as if he rather expected to see the loaf disappear under the efficacy of his wife’s petitions. “I ain’t a going to be blest out of house and home.
en: Cruncher, looking around as if he expected the loaf of bread to vanish because of her prayers. "I'm not going to be blessed out of my house and home.

raw: I won’t have my wittles blest off my table.
en: I won't have my food blessed off my table.

raw: Keep still!”
en: Keep quiet!"

raw: Exceedingly red-eyed and grim, as if he had been up all night at a party which had taken anything but a convivial turn, Jerry Cruncher worried his breakfast rather than ate it, growling over it like any four-footed inmate of a menagerie.
en: With red eyes and a grim face, looking as if he had been up all night at a very unpleasant gathering, Jerry Cruncher grumbled through his breakfast like a wild animal in a zoo.

raw: Towards nine o’clock he smoothed his ruffled aspect, and, presenting as respectable and business-like an exterior as he could overlay his natural self with, issued forth to the occupation of the day.
en: Around nine o'clock, he smoothed down his hair, put on the most respectable and business-like look he could manage, and headed out for the day's work.

raw: It could scarcely be called a trade, in spite of his favourite description of himself as “a honest tradesman.” His stock consisted of a wooden stool, made out of a broken-backed chair cut down, which stool, young Jerry, walking at his father’s side, carried every morning to beneath the banking-house window that was nearest Temple Bar: where, with the addition of the first handful of straw that could be gleaned from any passing vehicle to keep the cold and wet from the odd-job-man’s feet, it formed the encampment for the day.
en: It could hardly be called a business, despite his favorite description of himself as an "honest tradesman." His equipment consisted of a wooden stool made from an old chair. Young Jerry carried this stool at his father’s side every morning to a spot beneath the bank window closest to Temple Bar. There, with a handful of straw gathered from passing carriages to keep the cold and wet off his feet, Jerry set up his spot for the day.

raw: On this post of his, Mr.
en: At this post, Mr.

raw: Cruncher was as well known to Fleet-street and the Temple, as the Bar itself,--and was almost as in-looking.
en: Cruncher was as well known to the people of Fleet Street and the Temple as the Temple Bar gate itself, and he looked almost as dark and gloomy.

raw: Encamped at a quarter before nine, in good time to touch his three-cornered hat to the oldest of men as they passed in to Tellson’s, Jerry took up his station on this windy March morning, with young Jerry standing by him, when not engaged in making forays through the Bar, to inflict bodily and mental injuries of an acute description on passing boys who were small enough for his amiable purpose.
en: Set up by a quarter to nine, in time to tip his hat to the senior clerks as they entered Tellson’s, Jerry took his post on this windy March morning. Young Jerry stood by him when he wasn't running off to tease and annoy smaller boys on the street.

raw: Father and son, extremely like each other, looking silently on at the morning traffic in Fleet-street, with their two heads as near to one another as the two eyes of each were, bore a considerable resemblance to a pair of monkeys.
en: Father and son, looking remarkably alike, stood silently watching the morning traffic on Fleet Street. With their heads close together, they looked a bit like a pair of monkeys.

raw: The resemblance was not lessened by the accidental circumstance, that the mature Jerry bit and spat out straw, while the twinkling eyes of the youthful Jerry were as restlessly watchful of him as of everything else in Fleet-street.
en: The comparison was made even stronger by the fact that the older Jerry chewed and spat out straw, while the younger Jerry watched him and the street with restless, twinkling eyes.

raw: The head of one of the regular indoor messengers attached to Tellson’s establishment was put through the door, and the word was given:
en: Just then, the head of one of the bank's indoor messengers appeared at the door, and he called out:

raw: “Porter wanted!”
en: "Messenger needed!"

raw: “Hooray, father!
en: "Hooray, father!

raw: Here’s an early job to begin with!”
en: Here's an early job to start the day!"

raw: Having thus given his parent God speed, young Jerry seated himself on the stool, entered on his reversionary interest in the straw his father had been chewing, and cogitated.
en: Wishing his father luck, young Jerry sat down on the stool, took over the straw his father had been chewing, and began to think.

raw: “Al-ways rusty!
en: "Always rusty!

raw: His fingers is al-ways rusty!” muttered young Jerry. “Where does my father get all that iron rust from?
en: His fingers are always rusty!" muttered young Jerry. "Where does my father get all that iron rust from?

raw: He don’t get no iron rust here!”
en: He certainly doesn't get it around here!"
